title: Dynamics of the Type I PLL
intro: A linear model of the simple PLL in the phase domain, its second-order response, and the trade-offs among settling speed, ripple, phase error and stability (Razavi, Section 16.1.3).

blocks.text: Assume the loop is locked and look only at excess phases $\Phi_{in}$, $\Phi_{out}$. The PD is a subtractor with gain $K_{PD}$, the filter is $1/(1 + s/\omega_{LPF})$ and the VCO is $K_{VCO}/s$:
One pole at the origin makes this a type I loop. Its loop gain is infinite at DC, so slow input phase changes are copied exactly to the output. Closing the loop:

Because frequency is the derivative of phase, the same $H(s)$ relates input and output frequency, and since $\omega_{out}$ follows $V_{cont}$, watching $V_{cont}$ after an input frequency step shows the closed-loop response directly.

blocks.alt: Four step responses rising to one: zeta 0.2 overshoots strongly and rings for a long time, zeta 0.5 overshoots modestly, zeta 0.707 slightly, and zeta 1 rises smoothly without overshoot.
blocks.caption: Step responses of a second-order loop at constant $\omega_n$.

blocks.text: The decay rate is $\zeta\omega_n$, and in the type I loop it is fixed by the filter alone:

A lower $\omega_{LPF}$ removes more ripple from the control line but settles more slowly. $\zeta$ below 0.5 rings badly; designs use $\zeta \ge \sqrt{2}/2$ or even 1 to allow for spread (some applications need far more to avoid peaking in $H$).

items: Ripple vs settling: both set by $\omega_{LPF}$.
Phase error vs stability: the static error $\Delta\omega/(K_{PD}K_{VCO})$ and $\zeta$ both fall as $K_{PD}K_{VCO}$ rises.

blocks.text: The Bode plot shows the same thing: the loop gain falls at 20 dB/dec up to $\omega_{LPF}$ and 40 dB/dec beyond, with phase going from −90° to −180°. Raising $K_{PD}K_{VCO}$ lifts the whole magnitude curve, pushing the crossover to where the phase is closer to −180°. On the root locus, the open-loop poles at 0 and $-\omega_{LPF}$ meet at $-\omega_{LPF}/2$ when $K_{PD}K_{VCO} = \omega_{LPF}/4$ ($\zeta = 1$), then split vertically with their real part stuck at $-\omega_{LPF}/2$; the angle $\psi$ of the poles from the negative real axis satisfies $\cos\psi = \zeta$.

For a frequency step, $\Phi_{in} = \Delta\omega/s^2$, and the final-value theorem gives a phase error of $2\zeta\Delta\omega/\omega_n = \Delta\omega/(K_{PD}K_{VCO})$, matching the static result. A charge pump removes this error, which is the main reason for the next topic.

blocks.title: Choosing the loop gain
blocks.text: A type I PLL has $\omega_{LPF} = 2\pi \times 200\text{ kHz}$ and should have $\zeta = 0.707$. Find $K_{PD}K_{VCO}$, $\omega_n$ and the decay rate.
solution: $\zeta\omega_n = \omega_{LPF}/2 = 6.28\times10^5\text{ s}^{-1}$, a time constant of 1.6 µs.

blocks.title: Settling time
blocks.text: A type I loop with $\omega_{LPF} = 2\pi \times 50\text{ kHz}$ must hop by 1 MHz and settle within 1 kHz. Estimate the settling time, taking the worst case of the sinusoid and ignoring the $1/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$ factor.

blocks.title: Phase error after a frequency step
blocks.text: $K_{PD}K_{VCO} = 2\pi \times 10\text{ MHz}$ (in rad/s per rad). The input frequency steps by 2 MHz. What is the new steady-state phase error change?

blocks.title: Phase margin
blocks.text: For $\zeta = 0.707$ ($K_{PD}K_{VCO} = \omega_{LPF}/2$), find the gain crossover and phase margin of the open loop.
solution: Phase $= -90^{\circ} - \tan^{-1}0.455 = -114.5^{\circ}$, so the phase margin is 65.5°.
